cases.learnTitle: Vessel segments of the left coronary system (expert-outlined)
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (one hospital's catheterisation laboratory); no individual history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: The SYNTAX vessel segments (5 outlined here) were marked as polygons in CVAT by interventional cardiologists: one initial annotator for each image, cross-validated by two senior doctors, with the consensus as the label. The paper reports that the segment masks cover roughly 60-80% of the visible vessels and that annotators disagreed mostly at segment borders and on small vessels. The projection angle is not distributed.
cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is. The experts' labels on this frame are the vessel segments only; no narrowing regions are distributed for it.

cases.learnTitle: Narrowings of the left coronary system (expert-marked region)
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (one hospital's catheterisation laboratory); no individual history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: The SYNTAX vessel segments (6 outlined here) and 2 narrowings of 50% or more were marked as polygons in CVAT by interventional cardiologists: one initial annotator for each image, cross-validated by two senior doctors, with the consensus as the label. The paper reports that the segment masks cover roughly 60-80% of the visible vessels and that annotators disagreed mostly at segment borders and on small vessels. The projection angle is not distributed.
cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis.

cases.referenceSummary: The SYNTAX vessel segments (5 outlined here) were marked as polygons in CVAT by interventional cardiologists: one initial annotator for each image, cross-validated by two senior doctors, with the consensus as the label. The paper reports that the segment masks cover roughly 60-80% of the visible vessels and that annotators disagreed mostly at segment borders and on small vessels. The projection angle is not distributed.
cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is. The experts' labels on this frame are the vessel segments only; no narrowing regions are distributed for it.

cases.learnTitle: Narrowing of the left coronary system (expert-marked region)
cases.contextSource: Dataset description (one hospital's catheterisation laboratory); no individual history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: The SYNTAX vessel segments (6 outlined here) and the narrowing of 50% or more were marked as polygons in CVAT by interventional cardiologists: one initial annotator for each image, cross-validated by two senior doctors, with the consensus as the label. The paper reports that the segment masks cover roughly 60-80% of the visible vessels and that annotators disagreed mostly at segment borders and on small vessels. The projection angle is not distributed.
cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis.

cases.contextSource: Dataset description (one hospital's catheterisation laboratory); no individual history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: The SYNTAX vessel segments (4 outlined here) and the narrowing of 50% or more were marked as polygons in CVAT by interventional cardiologists: one initial annotator for each image, cross-validated by two senior doctors, with the consensus as the label. The paper reports that the segment masks cover roughly 60-80% of the visible vessels and that annotators disagreed mostly at segment borders and on small vessels. cases.learnNotes: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis.

A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is.

tasks.title: Find the narrowings
tasks.prompt: Read this coronary angiogram. Mark every narrowing of an artery of 50% or more that you find (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the regions are the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. tasks.title: Find the narrowing
tasks.prompt: Read this coronary angiogram. Mark every narrowing of an artery of 50% or more that you find (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.title: Find the narrowing
tasks.prompt: Read this coronary angiogram. Mark every narrowing of an artery of 50% or more that you find (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. tasks.explanation: Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. The SYNTAX score numbers the segments 1-4 and 16-16c for the right system and 5-15 for the left; the numbers are what cardiologists use to say where a narrowing is.

tasks.title: Find the narrowing
tasks.prompt: Read this coronary angiogram. Mark every narrowing of an artery of 50% or more that you find (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. tasks.title: Find the narrowings

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the regions are the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the region is the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.

Two arteries arise from the aortic root. The right coronary artery is usually a single long vessel that runs down the right side of the heart and curves under it to the back wall; it gives the posterior descending artery and, in most people, the posterolateral branches. The left main artery is a short trunk that divides into the left anterior descending artery (down the front of the heart towards the apex, with diagonal branches) and the left circumflex artery (round the left side, with obtuse marginal branches); sometimes a third, intermediate branch arises between them. tasks.title: Find the narrowings

hints.text: Follow each artery from the catheter outwards and compare the width of the contrast column with the normal vessel beside it.
Look for a short pinch, a long tapering or an irregular edge, in the main arteries first and then the larger branches.

tasks.explanation: A coronary stenosis is a narrowing of the lumen of an artery, most often from atherosclerotic plaque in the wall. An invasive angiogram shows only the lumen, filled with contrast, so a stenosis appears as a place where the bright column of contrast becomes narrower than the normal vessel next to it: a short pinch, a long tapering, or an irregular edge. Its degree is the percentage loss of diameter against that normal reference. The experts of this dataset marked regions with a narrowing of 50% or more in vessels at least 1.5 mm wide, judged with the angiography system's measuring software and by eye. Whether a narrowing limits blood flow also depends on its length, its place and the territory it supplies, which a single frame cannot tell you. Pitfalls: a vessel seen end-on or overlapped by another vessel hides or imitates a narrowing, so every artery is looked at in several projections; the catheter tip and the spine can cover the first centimetres of a vessel; and slow filling or poor mixing of contrast can make a normal vessel look pinched. The dataset does not label every visible narrowing or every vessel, so a narrowing you can see without a marked region is not necessarily a mistake. This is teaching material, not a diagnosis. On this frame the regions are the experts' marking; counting is in image pixels because no pixel size is distributed.
